intro: A darker edition: haunted houses, historical conspiracies, saints and miracles, horror gaming, and two deep dives into Westeros. Eight October picks plus two late-September lore discussions; spoilers are flagged in the summaries.

items.title: Inside the Most Violent Haunted Houses
items.summary: The Why Files revisits three alleged hauntings, including cases in Gary, Indiana, and Atchison, Kansas. Accounts of poltergeist activity, unsettling voices and physical attacks provide the campfire-story atmosphere.
items.why: This is close to the spooky storytelling you asked for: disturbing cases, witnesses and the question of what actually happened behind the stories.

items.title: Was the Titanic switched with its sister ship?
items.summary: AJ explores the Titanic–Olympic switch theory, following claims about insurance, J.P. Morgan and the wreck's identity. The episode presents a historical conspiracy narrative; the alleged switch is not an established fact.
items.why: A proper Why Files rabbit hole: a familiar event recast as a hidden plot, with enough concrete historical details to give you something to investigate.

items.title: The Last Sign: 3I/ATLAS and the Hopi Blue Star
items.summary: Today's Why Files episode explores accounts of Hopi end-times prophecy and a proposed connection with interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. The connection is the episode's speculative interpretation, rather than an astronomical finding.
items.why: It combines your interest in prophecy, unusual celestial events and ancient traditions. A chance to examine how another tradition's signs are interpreted alongside modern events.

items.title: A Roswell witness affidavit resurfaces in the UFO files
items.summary: Unexplained Mysteries reports that a newly released contractor report includes testimony matching Walter Haut's earlier Roswell affidavit. The account alleges a craft and bodies; its appearance in a released file does not independently authenticate those claims.
items.why: The interesting thread is how old testimony enters new official disclosures: precisely the sort of evidence-versus-presentation question that makes UFO secrecy worth examining.

items.title: What does 'the communion of saints' actually mean?
items.summary: Andrew Davison examines holiness, fellowship and sharing in the saints' good works. Drawing on Aquinas, Augustine and the Westminster Confession, he explores both communion among holy people and participation in holy things.
items.why: Directly relevant to your questions about the saints and the unity of Christ's people. Aquinas's account of sharing in others' good works gives you a particularly useful line of study.

items.title: St Winifred, a healing spring and 1,300 years of pilgrimage
items.summary: Camilla Harrison visits Holywell in Wales and reflects on water, pilgrimage and faith. She recounts St Winifred's miraculous restoration as hagiographic tradition and describes the continuing practice of immersion at her well.
items.why: A meeting of Christian devotion, miracle traditions and an ancient British sacred place—something to explore alongside your interest in saints and the supernatural.

items.title: The Doom mod whose anonymous creator never broke character
items.summary: A new retrospective explores MyHouse.wad, the 2023 Doom II mod that turns a suburban home into an impossible, changing labyrinth. Its fictional backstory and elusive creator make discovering the mod part of the horror. The article contains spoilers.
items.why: Retro gaming with an unsettling mystery at its centre, plus ingenious level design to pick apart. The 'how did they do that?' factor should appeal as much as the scares.

items.title: A free haunted-house horror game from The Mortuary Assistant's creator
items.summary: Playable Archive salvages a short psychological-horror experience from a cancelled project. PC Gamer describes found-footage storytelling, a dilapidated house and an estimated 30–60-minute playtime; the game is available free on Steam.
items.why: An immediately playable spooky discovery for an evening, with a mystery to unravel and no large time commitment. The article includes comments from its creator about preserving the abandoned project.

items.category: A Song of Ice and Fire
items.title: Harrenhal: the tournament where the Targaryen world came apart
items.summary: History of Westeros walks through The Mad King stage play, comparing its Harrenhal scenes with the books. Rhaegar, Lyanna, Howland Reed, Ashara Dayne and Aerys converge in a discussion full of book and play spoilers.
items.why: A dense Westeros-history rabbit hole, connecting the characters and hidden tensions behind Robert's Rebellion. Especially useful if you want the play's additions without attending a performance.

items.category: A Song of Ice and Fire
items.title: Fire & Blood versus House of the Dragon: changes, consequences and theories
items.summary: History of Westeros compares the adaptation with its source material, revisits earlier changes and considers which characters have diverged most. The discussion includes season-four theories and spoilers through season three.
items.why: For the analytical side of your ASOIAF interest: tracing how small changes affect motives, history and the larger story, with theories to weigh against the books.
